claims.text: Conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloys typically have a dual-phase microstructure containing a ductile FCC phase and a harder BCC-type phase.
The interphase boundaries in the conventionally cast baseline are incoherent.
Hot working followed immediately by rapid quenching constitutes a single-step thermomechanical intervention.
Controlled hot working followed by rapid quenching will produce a high density of mechanical twins in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Controlled hot working followed by rapid quenching will make FCC/BCC interphase boundaries more coherent.
Heat and deformation during hot working promote mechanical twinning.
Hot working improves FCC/BCC interphase-boundary coherence.
Twin boundaries impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Mechanical twinning contributes to strain hardening in an Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy under dynamic loading.
Twins provide additional deformation pathways that delay strain localization and improve ductility.
More coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries contribute to the simultaneous improvement of strength and ductility.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the treatment will increase yield strength.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, the treatment will increase tensile elongation.
The predicted simultaneous improvement should occur under quasi-static tensile loading at room temperature in eutectic high-entropy alloys with similar phase compositions.
High-strain-rate loading, elevated temperatures, or substantially different alloy chemistries may not produce the same improvements.
The magnitude of the improvements depends on hot-working temperature, strain rate, and quenching rate.
A cast control and a thermomechanically treated group can be compared by room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing and TEM or EBSD characterization.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in both yield strength and elongation, or failure to observe the proposed microstructural mediators, would falsify the hypothesis.
